'''''Berberis bealei''''',  also known as '''leatherleaf mahonia''', '''Beale's barberry''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=MABE2|taxon=Mahonia bealei|accessdate=28 June 2015}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/berberis-bealei/|title=Berberis bealei (Leatherleaf Mahonia) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu|access-date=2020-02-28}}</ref> is a species of evergreen<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |first1=Veit Martin |last1=Dörken |last2=Sarazin |first2=Andreas |title=''Mahonia bealei'' – Beales Mahonie (Berberidaceae) und weitere Mahonien |url=https://www.botanik-bochum.de/jahrbuch/Pflanzenportraet_Mahonia_bealei.pdf |year=2017 |journal=Jahrbuch des Bochumer Botanischen Vereins |volume=8 |pages=270-276}}</ref> shrub native to mainland China.<ref name="eggroll">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200008385 Flora of China v 19 p 778, ''Mahonia bealei'']</ref> The species has been regarded as the same species as ''[[Berberis japonica]]'', native to Taiwan, but the two differ consistently in certain floral and leaf characters. Both species are widely cultivated in many countries as ornamentals. ''Berberis bealei'' has reportedly [[escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] and become established in the wild in scattered places in the south-eastern United States from [[Arkansas]] to [[Florida]] to [[Delaware]].<ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Mahonia%20bealei.png Biota of North America Program]</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=233500224 Flora of North America vol 3, ''Berberis bealei'']</ref>

== Description ==
''Berberis bealei'' is a multi-stemmed, evergreen shrub or small tree with irregular, strong upright stems that have limited branching. It grows up to {{convert|8|m}} tall, is upright, and is scarcely branching. Leatherleaf mahonia has pinnate compound leave evergreen leaves. The [[leaves]] are up to {{Convert|50|cm}} long, with 4–10 pairs of [[Leaflet (botany)|leaflets]], plus a much larger terminal leaflet. The sessile leaflets have spines and the terminal leaflets are larger than others.

Flowering occurs in late winter and early spring, when fragrant, lemon-yellow flowers develop.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |title=Plant Details – Tennessee Invasive Plant Council |url=https://www.tnipc.org/invasive-plants/plant-details/ |access-date=2020-11-02 |language=en-US}}</ref> The flowers are borne in an erect [[raceme]] up to {{Convert|30|cm|abbr=on}} long. Showy but weakly foetid, yellow blooms appear in the late winter. Abundant grape-like fruits appear in late summer.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Berberis bealei (Leatherleaf Mahonia, Oregon Grape) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/berberis-bealei/ |access-date=2020-11-02 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> The berries emerge by the beginning of winter and are blue or dark purple colored egg-shaped berries, up to {{Convert|15|mm|frac=8}} long, that turn bluish black with a grayish bloom. Fruits hang in grapelike clusters and are glaucous, covered with a white waxy coating.<ref name=":02" /> The erect stems are stiff and unbranched.<ref name=":02" /><ref name="eggroll" /><ref>[http://www.botanicus.org/page/1430755 Carrière, Élie Abel. 1855. Flore des Serres et des Jardins de l'Europe 10: 166 ''Mahonia bealei'']</ref><ref>[http://www.botanicus.org/page/212044 Fedde, Friedrich Karl Georg. 1901. Botanische Jahrbücher für Systematik, Pflanzengeschichte und Pflanzengeographie 31(1): 119–120, ''Mahonia japonica'' var. ''bealei'']</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Fortune |first=Robert |date=1850 |title=Notes of a traveller – No. X. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/101140#page/219/mode/1up |journal=Gardeners' Chronicle & Agricultural Gazette |volume=1850 |pages=212 |via=Biodiversity Heritage Library}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

== Etymology ==
First collected in [[Anhui]], [[China]] by [[Robert Fortune]], the plants were taken to [[Shanghai]], where they were planted in the garden of Mr. Beale to await transportation to Europe. Fortune named the species after Beale in an issue of the ''[[The Gardeners' Chronicle|Gardeners' Chronicle]]'' and was sure it was a distinct species, separate from ''[[Berberis japonica]]''.<ref name=":0" /> ''Chronicle'' editor [[John Lindley]] was unconvinced and repeatedly referred to the new species as ''Berberis'' (''Mahonia'') ''japonica''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bayton|first=Ross|date=2017|title=The identity of Mahonia japonica|journal=The Plantsman |series=New Series|volume=16 |issue=4|pages=244–248}}</ref> The confusion between ''B. japonica'' and ''B. bealei'' is reflected in subsequent literature, with the latter referred to variously as ''B. japonica'' var. ''bealei'', ''B. japonica'' 'Bealei' or ''B. japonica'' Bealei [[Cultivar group|Group]]. Plants labelled as ''B. bealei'' with silver undersides to the leaves have been recognized as the [[cultivar]] 'Silver Back', though the original Fortune plants lack this silver colouration. As such, 'Silver Back' may represent a different species.

''Berberis bealei'' is one of approximately 70 species that were once classified in genus ''[[Mahonia]]''. Thus, older sources refer to this species as ''Mahonia bealei'' or ''M. Japonica''.

==Distribution and habitat==
''Berberis bealei'' is native to China ([[Anhui]], [[Fujian]], [[Guangdong]], [[Guangxi]], [[Henan]], [[Hubei]], [[Hunan]], [[Jiangsu]], [[Jiangxi]], [[Shaanxi]], [[Sichuan]], [[Zhejiang]]) and was brought to Europe in the 1800s.<ref name="tnipc.org">{{Cite web|title=Plant Details – Tennessee Invasive Plant Council|url=https://www.tnipc.org/invasive-plants/plant-details/|access-date=2020-10-14|language=en-US}}</ref> It has been planted as an ornamental plant throughout Europe and the United States. Birds eat the seeds of this plant and spread them widely. ''Berberis bealei'' is established in the southern U.S.<ref name="tnipc.org"/> ''Berberis bealei'' is particularly common in bottomland forests and grows well in shade to partial shade. It may not flower if it does not receive at least a few hours of sun each day and does not like hot, midday sun in the southern zones.<ref name=":02"/> The shrub's ability to tolerate many sites, and the fact that birds disperse the berries, has allowed it to naturalize in parts of the U.S.<ref name=":02"/>

== Invasiveness ==
As is the case with many invasive species, ''B. bealei'' was introduced intentionally for purpose of landscaping. ''Berberis bealei'' needs to be closely monitored as an invasive species. The spiny leaves of ''B. bealei'' deter them from being eaten by omnivores such as whitetail deer.<ref name="Maryland Invasive Species Council">{{Cite web |last=Maryland Invasive Species Council |date=6 July 2010 |title=It is Not Holly {{!}} Maryland Invasive Species Council |url=http://mdinvasives.org/iotm/july-2010/ |access-date=2020-11-03 |language=en-US}}</ref> Suggested control methods include pulling the seedlings, cutting the mature plants to stumps repeatedly, and using herbicides.<ref name="Maryland Invasive Species Council" /> ''Berberis bealei'' is considered invasive in the Southeastern U.S., specifically [[Alabama]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[North Carolina]], [[South Carolina]], [[Michigan]], and [[Tennessee]].<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":4" />

== Cultivation ==
''Berberis bealei'' is winter hardy to [[Hardiness zone|USDA Zones]] 7–9 where it is easily grown in moist, well-drained soils in part shade (morning sun or sun dappled shade) to full shade. Also tolerates full sun (albeit often with some bleaching of foliage colors), but only in the cooler northern parts of its growing range. Established plants tolerate some soil dryness and drought.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Mahonia bealei - Plant Finder|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=277789&isprofile=0&pt=2|access-date=2020-11-03|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> ''Berberis bealei'' grows in locations protected from exposure to strong winds. Plants will spread by suckering and seed. Unless naturalization is desired, suckers should be promptly removed as they appear. Single specimen shrubs may fruit poorly. Growing more than one shrub together results in the best fruit production. It is easily propagated from cuttings or seed<ref name=":3" /> though is considered invasive in the mid-Atlantic and [[Southeastern U.S.]]

== Uses ==
''Berberis bealei'' has been used to treat infections such as [[strep throat]] and [[tuberculosis]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Wild Edible Wednesday 1/9 - Leatherleaf Mahonia |url=https://www.sarcraft.com/news/leatherleaf-mahonia |access-date=2020-10-14 |website=SARCRAFT |language=en-US}}</ref> This plant can also be used to treat bacterial infections such as [[dysentery]] and food poisoning.<ref name=":2" /> ''Berberis bealei'' is also high in [[tannin]]s and may help muscle pain, [[arthritis]], and aches associated with fever.<ref name=":2" /> Fruits are boiled and strained for medicinal preparations.  Plants of the genus ''Berberis'' have long been used as medicine in China as a treatment for [[periodontitis]], dysentery, tuberculosis and wounds.

''Berberis bealei'' has berries that are used in pies, jellies, jams, beverages and confections. The yellow flowers are eaten or used to make a lemonade-like drink.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last1=beverage |first1=DEANE in |last2=C |last3=y |last4=Raw |first4=Edible |last5=Flowers |last6=Fruits/Berries |last7=Herb |first7=Greens/Pot |last8=Jam/Jelly |last9=Uses |first9=Plant |date=2013-02-14 |title=Mahonia Mélange |url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/mahonia-melange/ |access-date=2020-11-03 |website=Eat The Weeds and other things, too |language=en-US}}</ref> If these berries are fermented and distilled they can make a wine. Ripe fruit of ''B. bealei'' are too acidic to eat raw but can be mixed with sugars or other berries. Young leaves are simmered in water can be eaten.<ref name=":12" /> ''Berberis bealei'' is not toxic in small amounts, just acidic. The berries can be eaten raw but the seed to pulp ratio is large so most of these berries are boiled and strained.
